system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-06-24 22:44:00 to 2172-06-26 17:23:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for two weeks of diffuse abdominal pain and bilious vomiting, initially attributed to constipation. Imaging showed no acute abdominal pathology, and symptoms improved with bowel regimen and enemas, supporting opioid-induced constipation as the cause. A urine culture grew E. coli, leading to a three-day course of Bactrim for a mild UTI. Her INR was monitored due to Coumadin interaction. Chronic conditions including HIV, hepatitis B/C, diastolic heart failure, and a healing left tibial fracture were stable. Orthopedics cleared her for 50% weight-bearing. She was discharged home with services, instructed to complete antibiotics, monitor INR, follow up with orthopedics, and maintain bowel regimen.
problems: Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of ovary

microbiology.comments: HIV-1 RNA is not detected.  Performed using the ___ HIV-1 Test v2.0.  Detection Range: 20-10,000,000 copies/mL.  This test is approved for monitoring HIV-1 viral load in known HIV-positive patients. It is not approved for diagnosis of acute HIV infection.  In symptomatic acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), the viral load is usually very high (>>1000 copies/mL). If acute HIV infection is clinically suspected and there is a detectable but low viral load, please contact the laboratory for interpretation.  It is recommended that any NEW positive HIV-1 viral load result, in the absence of positive serology, be confirmed by submitting a new sample FOR HIV-1 PCR, in addition to serological testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this bad headache for two or three days. It’s in my forehead and wraps around the front. It feels just like my migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any sensitivity to light or nausea with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can’t stand the lights. I’ve been keeping a towel over my eyes. I also feel hot and sweaty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took my temperature today—it was 101. I’ve also had burning when I pee for weeks, and my left leg has been red and sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for sharing that. We’ll check your labs and do a CT scan of your head to make sure there’s nothing serious going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan came back clear—no bleeding or stroke. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But the headache is still really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is high, and you have a fever. We’re concerned about infection—possibly in your urine or leg. But because of the headache and fever, we also need to rule out meningitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Meningitis? That sounds scary. What do you need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A lumbar puncture—spinal tap—would help us check. But given your weight and high INR, it’s riskier. And you can refuse if you’re uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not. I’ve had one before—it was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll start antibiotics just in case—ceftriaxone and moxifloxacin—since you’re allergic to vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but can I get something for the headache? I ran out of my Imitrex at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give you a dose now. If it helps, that would support it being a migraine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the headache now, about 20 minutes after the Imitrex?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still there, but not as sharp. Lights don’t bother me as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. It suggests this is likely a migraine. But we still need to treat the infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture grew E. coli, sensitive to Bactrim. So we’ll continue antibiotics for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not too much. It’s common for you. But we also think your left leg infection—cellulitis—is contributing to the fever and high white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The redness goes up to my knee. There’s a little scab on my shin—maybe that’s where it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s likely the entry point. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for both the UTI and cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds? I stopped them because I was nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart them before you go home. Your last viral load was undetectable, so staying on track is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood thinner? I’m on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was high—4.8—so we held Coumadin for safety. We’ll restart it at discharge, but you’ll need an INR check soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics affect it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, possibly. That’s why we need to monitor it closely and adjust your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—from 13.8 to 8.2. That means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg? It’s less red today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the swelling and redness are improving. We’ll send you home with a seven-day course of Bactrim and cephalexin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both? Why two?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bactrim covers the UTI, and cephalexin is better for skin infections like cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my headache hasn’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ve stopped the meningitis antibiotics since your symptoms improved with Imitrex and we found other infection sources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish both antibiotics. Restart your HIV meds. Take Coumadin as before, but get your INR checked in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Imitrex?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have nine tablets—take one as needed for migraines. Call if you need more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than three pounds. Also, follow up with your doctors for blood cultures and HIV viral load results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have a nurse go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in. Still feeling okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember to take your meds, check your INR, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a severe frontal headache, fever, and elevated white blood cell count. The headache responded well to Imitrex, supporting a diagnosis of migraine, though initial concern for meningitis led to empiric antibiotics, later discontinued. She was found to have cellulitis in the left lower leg and a urinary tract infection caused by E. coli, both treated with appropriate antibiotics. Her INR was elevated on admission, so Coumadin was held and later restarted at discharge. HIV medications were resumed, and she was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics, monitor INR, and follow up on pending lab results.
